Co-creator Jim Howick told the BBC that the writers felt the same impulse to collaborate again as they did following the end of Horrible Histories and the Ghosts TV series. Asked about what lies ahead for the group in light of these comments, Willbond told The Independent:  “I really hope we can devise something and sell something else, but it's really hard at the moment. title: In The Room | Why France is rioting – and is Britain next?
description: France is reeling after a weekend of unrest that escalated dramatically. Hundreds of thousands marched peacefully, but elsewhere shops were looted, cars burned, police attacked and public buildings set alight. What began with schoolchildren furious about missing teachers, crumbling classrooms and a system they believe is failing them quickly became something much bigger. People of all ages joined demonstrations driven by anger over the cost of living, deteriorating public services and a future that feels increasingly out of reach. With France approaching a presidential election, the unrest exposes a deeper political crisis. But this is not just a French story. Across Europe, established parties are struggling to retain the confidence of increasingly disillusioned electorates. And Britain has experienced its own moments when public anger has spilled into violence. Helen MacNamara, who was inside government during the 2011 riots and has attended countless COBR meetings, examines what happens when governments begin to lose control of the streets, and what France's crisis might tell us about the pressures building closer to home. New episodes of In The Room come out weekly. Listen to the latest on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, or watch on YouTube.

title: Wombs of Debt | The dark human cost behind the world’s sugar industry
description: In India’s sugarcane fields, missing a single day of work can trap an entire family in inescapable debt. For thousands of women, keeping pace with the harvest has come at a devastating physical cost: their wombs. In Wombs of Debt, producer and director Noopur Jambheker and producer Mohammad Dawood travel to Maharashtra’s Beed district to uncover the harrowing human cost behind a global cash crop. To eliminate menstrual cycles, avoid pregnancy, and guarantee they never miss a day in the field, thousands of young women undergo surgical hysterectomies. In Beed district, the hysterectomy rate stands at 17%—more than five times India’s national average. Over the past decade alone, more than 13,000 women in the region have undergone the procedure. Watch the full investigation to witness their stories and see the real cost of the sugar. title: Why are we so obsessed with the 1990s?
description: Kate Moss, Naomi Campbell, Tracey Emin and Alexander McQueen: our fascination with the 1990s shows no sign of fading. But a new exhibition at Tate Britain, The 90s: Art and Fashion, challenges the nostalgia surrounding the decade. “The Cool Britannia moment, which was a campaign to promote Britain as this youth-driven, optimistic, forward-facing nation, actually glossed over the lived realities of so many Britons at this time,” says Tate curator Helen Little. Little, who curated the exhibition alongside former Vogue editor Edward Enninful, suggests that the show invites audiences to look beyond a nostalgic view of the decade, even if nostalgia may be unavoidable for some visitors. Among the artists featured is Vinca Petersen, who documented the rise of rave culture, capturing free parties and travelling sound systems across Europe. “I felt that all the press about this scene and about travellers and about ravers was very negative,” says Petersen. The 1990s were far from perfect. Yet, coming after the end of the Cold War and before 9/11, the era carried a sense of freedom and possibility that can feel difficult to imagine today. Perhaps that is why we keep returning to the decade and why the exhibition is likely to draw large crowds.

Xander Butler, 23, of Willoughby Road, Ipswich, rushed at one of the officers, throwing her into a wall and placing an arm around her neck. He grabbed another officer, who had tried to intervene, from behind and wrapped an arm around her neck before punching her in the face. In a victim impact statement for the court, one officer wrote: “I remember thinking that if me and my colleague could not find a way to stop him, he could seriously hurt or even kill one of us." Butler was jailed for 16 months at Ipswich Crown Court on Thursday 1 October after pleading guilty to intentional strangulation, assault by beating of an emergency worker and criminal damage. A further count of both intentional strangulation and of assault by beating of an emergency worker was left on file after Butler pleaded not guilty to these offences.

The legendary broadcaster and campaigner’s death, at the age of 86, was announced by her family on Wednesday (30 September). Dame Esther became a strong proponent for assisted dying, after she was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023. Speaking to the BBC over the phone in an interview in March this year, Dame Esther said that although she was no longer having treatment, “things were improving”. She said: “The problem with me, according to my oncologist, is I am an outlier, I am living longer than he expected me to, No-one knows why, but the last scan things were improving, despite the drugs not working and not being treated.” Dame Esther said she had another scan booked for June, adding: “If I’m still improving I will carry on fighting, maybe it’s this battle that is keeping me going, who knows?”

Esther Rantzen reunites Nicholas Winton with dozens of children he saved in WWII in resurfaced clip after her death
description: This is the incredible moment Dame Esther Rantzen reunites an un-expecting Sir Nicholas Winton with dozens of the 669 Jewish children he saved from the Holocaust. The momentous moment aired during the famous 1988 broadcast of the BBC show That’s Life! which Dame Esther hosted. It has now resurfaced following Dame Esther’s death on Wednesday (30 September) at the age of 86. Sir Nicholas organized trains to evacuate children from Nazi-occupied Czechoslovakia to Britain in 1938 and 1939. He secured foster families for the children, but kept his work a secret for nearly 50 years. His actions only came to light when his wife found a forgotten scrapbook in their attic containing the children's names and photos. In February 1988, Sir Nicholas sat in the studio audience of That's Life!, believing he was just a member of the public. Dame Esther Rantzen then pulled out his scrapbook, revealing what he had done, before asking if anyone in the audience owed their life to him. This prompted dozens of adults seated all around him to stand up and applaud him.

In SAS: The Shadow War, The Independent’s international affairs editor Sam Kiley traces the regiment’s covert campaign against the IRA in Northern Ireland, from the surveillance operations and ambushes of the Troubles to the hard questions that still endure today. Along the way, the Iranian Embassy siege and a deadly operation in Gibraltar reveal how the SAS became both a celebrated and a contested force. Drawing on rare and previously unheard first-hand accounts from former operatives and those who witnessed the conflict up close, this eight-part documentary series explores a war fought largely out of sight – and the legal battle now being waged over how its actions should be judged.
